core.big_idea: Human disobedience damaged the good relationship God intended.

passages.reading_note: Read selected verses slowly; name the choices and consequences without graphic or shaming language.
Recall the good instruction God had already given.

core.metanarrative_position: Rebellion: people mistrust God, disobey His good instruction, and hide from Him.

claims.statement: God gave the first humans a clear instruction before their disobedience.
The serpent contradicted God, and the humans chose to eat what God had forbidden.
After disobeying, the humans experienced shame, fear, hiding, and blame.
Human sin involves mistrusting God and choosing our own way, not merely making an accidental mistake.

core.interpretation_skill: Retell the sequence; distinguish temptation, choice, and consequence; avoid adding details not in the passage.

learning.foundation_objective: Retell the main action in Genesis 3:1-13 and say that the people disobeyed God.
learning.extension_objective: Explain how mistrust led to disobedience and name one truthful response when we do wrong.
know: God had given a good instruction.
The people chose to disobey and then hid.
understand: Hiding and blame do not repair wrongdoing.
practise: Tell the truth when something has gone wrong.
Ask God and people for forgiveness instead of shifting blame.
become: A child who trusts God, tells the truth, and accepts responsibility.
success_evidence: The child places four story events in order.
The child identifies disobedience rather than fruit as the core problem.
The child names a truthful response to wrongdoing.

zero_prep_card.objective: Children retell the first disobedience and explain that mistrusting God damaged a good relationship.
zero_prep_card.opening: Ask: What is the difference between making a mistake and choosing to ignore a clear instruction?
say: God had given one clear instruction.
The serpent tried to make God seem untrustworthy.
The people chose their own way and then hid and blamed.
When we do wrong, God wants truth rather than hiding or blame.
ask: What did the serpent say about God’s words?
What happened after the people ate?
What can we do instead of hiding or blaming?
zero_prep_card.do: Use the Choice, Action, Consequence Cards to retell the story in order.
zero_prep_card.close: Pray: God, help us trust Your words, tell the truth, and turn back when we do wrong.
materials: Choice, Action, Consequence Cards or four blank sheets

preparation.passage_context: Genesis 3 follows a good creation and a clear boundary in Genesis 2. The narrative describes temptation, human choice, shame, fear, hiding, and blame.
text_observations: The serpent reframes God’s command and questions its truthfulness.
The woman and man both participate in the disobedience.
God questions the humans, and each response shifts responsibility.
interpretation_notes: Keep the focus on mistrust and disobedience, not on identifying the fruit.
Do not make Eve the sole cause; the text holds both humans accountable.
For younger children, use “choosing against God’s good instruction” before technical theories of sin.
theological_guardrails: Do not teach that every hardship is direct punishment for a child’s particular sin.
Do not ask children to disclose private wrongdoing publicly.
Do not present God as unable or unwilling to seek people who hide.

likely_questions.question: What kind of fruit was it?
likely_questions.purpose: State that the passage does not name the fruit; the important point is the forbidden choice.

likely_questions.question: Does God stop loving people when they do wrong?
likely_questions.purpose: Say that sin is serious, but the wider story shows God seeking, judging, and promising rescue.

discussion_questions.question: What had God actually said before the serpent spoke?
discussion_questions.extension_prompt: Compare the command with the serpent’s version.

discussion_questions.question: What choice did the humans make?
discussion_questions.extension_prompt: Explain why temptation did not remove responsibility.

discussion_questions.question: What changed immediately after the choice?
discussion_questions.extension_prompt: Separate explicit consequences from later synthesis.

discussion_questions.question: What is a truthful response when we do wrong?
discussion_questions.foundation_prompt: Tell the truth and ask forgiveness.
discussion_questions.extension_prompt: Explain why responsibility differs from shame-based self-condemnation.

activities.title: Choice, Action, Consequence Sort
steps: Add hiding and blame; retell the sequence.
activities.learning_link: Makes cause and effect concrete without reducing sin to an accidental mistake.
activities.low_resource_alternative: Write four headings on the board and let children point.

activities.title: Truth Instead of Blame
activities.learning_link: Connects the story to honest responsibility without inviting private disclosure.

closing.prayer_prompt: Ask for trust, truthfulness, and courage to turn back when wrong.
closing.take_home_line: God’s way is good; when we do wrong, we tell the truth and turn back.

family.title: Truth Instead of Hiding
family.parent_intro: Use this study to talk about trust and responsibility without asking for private confessions.

flow.instructions: Use the opening prompt to connect the lesson to ordinary family life.
Read Genesis 3:1-13, or retell it in four short parts for a younger child.
Ask what God said, what the people chose, and what they did next.
Use four objects to mark Instruction, Temptation, Choice, and Hiding; place them in order.
Choose the weekly action, then pray together.

questions: What can we say when we have done something wrong?

interactive.title: Four-Part Story
interactive.instructions: Place four household objects in story order and retell one sentence for each.

family.weekly_action: Use one truthful repair sentence this week: “I did it. I am sorry. How can I help put it right?”
family.prayer: God, help us trust You, tell the truth, and turn back when we do wrong.
family.parent_note: Keep examples ordinary and fictional; do not turn family study into an interrogation.

quiz.question: What had God given before the disobedience?
What did the people do after disobeying?
The passage says the fruit was an apple.
quiz.explanation: Genesis does not name the fruit.

quiz.question: Which is a truthful response to wrongdoing?
options: Tell the truth and seek repair

answer.text: Tell the truth and seek repair

quiz.explanation: Truth and responsibility oppose hiding and blame.

puzzle.title: What Happened Next?
puzzle.instructions: Put the four events in story order.

printables.title: Choice, Action, Consequence Cards
printables.purpose: Help children retell Genesis 3 as a sequence of instruction, temptation, choice, and consequence.

accessibility.reading_level: Short concrete sentences suitable for teacher-led reading with ages 4-8.
accessibility.plain_language_rule: Use concrete verbs and define every abstract term through the story.
neurodiversity_supports: Allow pointing, drawing, or one-word responses.
Give one direction at a time.
sensory_notes: Participation must not require loud noise, touch, or public performance.
non_reader_support: Use pictures, objects, or gesture-supported retelling.

do_not_ask: Do not ask children to confess private wrongdoing before the group.
Do not label a child as bad or compare children publicly.
safeguarding.teacher_response: Use fictional, low-stakes examples and distinguish responsible confession from humiliating disclosure.
